kurals.tamil:
பகைஎன்னும் பண்பி லதனை ஒருவன்
நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakaiennum panpi ladhanai oruvan
nakaiyeyum ventarpaatru andru.
kurals.meaning: Enmity is a thing with no goodness in it; no one should wish for it, not even as a game or a joke.
kurals.elementary: Some kids pretend to be enemies just for fun, teasing and picking fights as a joke. The poet says even pretend enmity is a bad game, because a joke fight can quickly turn into a real one that nobody can stop.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by naming its subject with a moral label: pakai (பகை, enmity) is panpiladhu (பண்பிலது), ‘that which is devoid of good quality’. The emphatic nakaiyeyum (நகையேயும், ‘even in jest / even in play’) carries the force of the couplet: enmity is not to be courted even in sport, still less in earnest. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as an evil without merit that should not be desired even as a pastime, and Kalaignar explains that enmity runs contrary to good character; Puliyur Kesigan adds that this is the settled conclusion of the ethical treatises. The placement is notable: in a chapter that goes on to give hard-headed advice about handling enemies, Valluvar first insists that enmity itself is never desirable. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net, which titles the chapter பகைத்திறந் தெரிதல் with a word break.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavad Gita’s list of divine qualities, Krishna includes adroha, freedom from malice or hostility, alongside forgiveness, fortitude, and purity.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats freedom from hostility as part of the character of one born to a divine nature, not just a matter of policy.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats enmity as a lack of good character, something never to be cultivated.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Thematically aligned on rejecting malice; the Gita does not address enmity ‘in jest’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Roman believers to do everything in their power to avoid hostility with anyone.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make avoiding enmity a standing rule, not an occasional courtesy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good general match; lacks the Kural’s specific warning about playful enmity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allāh and from prayer. So will you not desist?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that pastimes such as gambling are a doorway through which enmity and hatred enter a community.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise warns that enmity can creep in through play and should not be invited even there.
islam._accuracy_note: Shared idea of enmity arising from amusements; the Qur’an targets specific vices rather than jest in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares the person who harms a neighbour and then claims it was only a joke to a madman throwing deadly missiles.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts refuse to excuse hostility on the grounds that it was meant in fun.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on the specific point that harm done ‘in sport’ is no less dangerous.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening chapter of the Dhammapada the Buddha teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred, but only by non-hatred, and calls this an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Enmity feeds on itself; once started, it only grows by being answered in kind.
buddhism.tie_back: This explains why the Kural says not to start enmity even playfully: it does not end easily once begun.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; supports the danger of enmity but not the ‘even in jest’ emphasis.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eris, goddess of strife, threw a golden apple inscribed for the fairest among the goddesses at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis; the contest it provoked led to the Judgment of Paris and ultimately the Trojan War.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mischievous gesture, almost a prank, set off rivalries that ended in a ten-year war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a mythic warning that enmity started lightly can grow beyond anyone’s control, as the Kural implies.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative story rather than a stated principle; Eris acted from spite as much as play.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the buffoon as one who will not spare himself or anyone else if he can raise a laugh, and who says things a refined person would never say.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, humour that wounds others is a vice of excess, not harmless fun.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly refuses to treat hostility as acceptable just because it is done in jest.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Adjacent theme (hurtful jesting) rather than enmity itself; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
வில்லேர் உழவர் பகைகொளினும் கொள்ளற்க
சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Viller uzhavar pakaikolinum kollarka
soller uzhavar pakai.
kurals.meaning: Even if you must make enemies of warriors whose plough is the bow, never make enemies of the wise whose plough is the word.
kurals.elementary: A bully with big muscles can only hurt you while he is near you. But a clever person who writes and speaks well can tell your story to the whole town and to people years from now. So the poet says: if you must quarrel with anyone, never quarrel with the people who are good with words.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a celebrated agricultural metaphor: villēr uḻavar (வில்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the bow’, that is, warriors, while collēr uḻavar (சொல்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the word’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the latter as scholars, Solomon Pappaiah as writers, Kalaignar as learned people of verbal power; the older commentarial tradition, reflected in Pope’s gloss ‘ministers whose ploughs are words’, takes them as counsellors skilled in policy. The concessive kolinum (‘even if you incur’) does not recommend war with soldiers; it ranks dangers, implying that the harm of hostile counsel, satire or reputation outlasts and outreaches the harm of arms. The metaphor also suggests that both kinds of men ‘cultivate’ a harvest, and the harvest of words is wider. No variant readings appear between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Parikshit, irritated while hunting, draped a dead snake on the silent sage Shamika; the sage’s young son Shringi, hearing of the insult, pronounced a curse that the king would die by the serpent Takshaka within seven days, and it came to pass.
hinduism.explanation: A mighty king who could command armies was undone by the spoken word of a sage’s son.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatizes the Kural’s ranking: the enmity of those whose weapon is the word is more dangerous than that of armed men.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the sage’s power is spiritual curse rather than counsel or satire.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that the tongue, though small, can set a whole forest ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts recognise that words can do more damage than their size suggests.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the power-of-words theme but is a warning to restrain one’s own tongue, not advice about enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satirise against the (non-believing amongst the) Quraish, for (the satire) is more grievous to them than the hurt of an arrow.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet asked the poet Hassan ibn Thabit to answer the Quraysh in verse, saying satire wounded them more than arrows.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s comparison: the word cuts deeper than the bow.
islam._accuracy_note: Remarkably close word-versus-arrow comparison, though framed as using words against enemies.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
judaism.explanation: Speech is presented as carrying literal life-and-death power.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s caution about enemies who wield words rests on the same recognition.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a general statement about speech rather than about choosing enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that hostile speech provokes hostile speech in return and brings harm back on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: Provoking those who answer in words invites a retaliation the Kural warns is especially costly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Related idea of verbal retaliation; does not compare warriors and wordsmiths.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Achilles’ death, Ajax the mighty warrior and Ulysses the eloquent speaker both claimed his armour; the Greek leaders, swayed by Ulysses’ speech, awarded it to him, and the power of eloquence was shown to outweigh strength of arm.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid stages a contest between the man of the sword and the man of words, and the man of words wins.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s point that the one who ploughs with words is the more formidable opponent.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (warrior versus speaker); paraphrased rather than quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial Socrates says he fears his old accusers, including a comic poet, more than his present prosecutors, because their talk had filled the jurors’ minds with slander since childhood.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates recognised that reputations shaped by skilled talkers and writers are harder to fight than any formal charge.
philosophy.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s warning that the enmity of wordsmiths is the most damaging kind.

kurals.tamil:
ஏமுற் றவரினும் ஏழை தமியனாய்ப்
பல்லார் பகைகொள் பவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Emur ravarinum ezhai thamiyanaaip
pallaar pakaikol pavan.
kurals.meaning: A person who stands alone and still makes enemies of many is more foolish than someone who has lost their mind.
kurals.elementary: Picture one kid on the playground who has no friends on his side, yet goes around picking fights with every group. Even someone who is not thinking clearly would not do that. The poet says this is the silliest thing a person can do.
kurals.university: The comparison turns on ēmuṟṟavar (ஏமுற்றவர்), ‘those who are deluded or deranged’: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss them as the mad (பித்தர்), Kalaignar as the arrogant, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘the despised’. Ēḻai (ஏழை) here means ‘senseless, witless’, not ‘poor’, as all the commentators agree. Tamiyaṉāy (‘being alone’) and pallār (‘many’) set up the arithmetic: a man without allies who collects many enemies has made the one choice even a madman might avoid. Pappaiah applies it directly to a ruler (ஆட்சியாளன்), in keeping with the Porutpal setting. The text matches in both ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Ravana rejected the counsel of his brother Vibhishana to return Sita, insulted him, and drove him out; Vibhishana went over to Rama, leaving Ravana isolated against a growing alliance.
hinduism.explanation: Ravana’s pride turned his own kin into enemies while he already faced a powerful foe.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural’s figure of folly: alone, and multiplying his enemies.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good narrative illustration; canto numbering varies across editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a prudent king who counts his forces before taking on a stronger enemy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns exactly the one who skips this reckoning and takes on many while alone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the logic of weighing strength before conflict; used by Jesus as a parable about discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers not to fall into disputes among themselves, lest they lose courage and their strength depart.
islam.explanation: Internal quarrels are presented as a direct cause of weakness and defeat.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link isolation and many quarrels with the loss of strength.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; about disunity within a community rather than one person against many.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that the solitary person has no one to rely on when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s lone man facing many enemies is exactly the one Kohelet pities.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the vulnerability of being alone; does not address making enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sammodamana Jataka, a flock of quail escape a fowler’s net by lifting it together, but once they begin quarrelling they no longer cooperate and the fowler catches them.
buddhism.explanation: Unity protects; quarrelling leaves each bird alone and easily caught.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lone man with many enemies is in the position of the quarrelling quail.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Fable about unity and quarrels; an indirect fit to one-against-many.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his sons, a bundle of sticks cannot be broken while bound together, but each stick snaps easily on its own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Strength lies in having others with you; alone, anyone is easily broken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s solitary man who takes on many is the single stick.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Father and His Sons (tr. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek fable rather than myth; addresses unity, not the folly of many enemies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that even a band of thieves cannot accomplish anything if its members wrong one another, and that injustice makes a person at odds with others and even with himself.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows that hostility on all sides makes effective action impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats making enemies everywhere as self-defeating folly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Related argument about self-defeating hostility; framed around justice rather than strategy.

kurals.tamil:
பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடை யாளன்
தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakainatpaak kontozhukum panputai yaalan
thakaimaikkan thangitru ulaku.
kurals.meaning: The world rests secure in the greatness of the gracious person who turns enemies into friends and lives that way.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who gets pushed by someone, and instead of pushing back, invites that person to play and they become best friends. The poet says people like that are so great that the whole world is held together by them.
kurals.university: After three couplets warning against enmity, Valluvar names the ideal: the paṇpuṭaiyāḷaṉ (பண்புடையாளன், ‘man of noble character’) who conducts himself (oḻukum) by making pakai into naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship). Takaimai (தகைமை) is greatness or excellence, and taṅkiṟṟu ulaku (‘the world abides’) is a strong claim: the stability of the world itself depends on such people. Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the world resting in his magnanimity; Solomon Pappaiah reads it of a ruler who converts enemies and lives with them, so that the world falls within his greatness; Kalaignar has the whole world praising such a person; Sivayogi Sivakumar says the world endures through such honoured conduct. Pope renders it as ‘worthy rule can change his foes to friends’, keeping the political frame. The couplet links back to Chapter 87 and forward to the strategic advice in 875.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Vibhishana, brother of the enemy king Ravana, came seeking refuge, Rama overruled his advisers’ suspicions, accepted him as an ally, and declared that he would give protection to anyone who sought it.
hinduism.explanation: Rama turned a member of the enemy household into a trusted friend and partner.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s gracious person who makes friends of foes, and on whom the right order of the world rests.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit; Vibhishana was already estranged from Ravana, so not a pure enemy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands active goodwill toward enemies rather than retaliation.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold up treating an enemy with friendship as the mark of the highest character.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Jesus commands love regardless of outcome, while the Kural highlights the result of friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that answering hostility with goodness can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s ideal of turning enmity into friendship.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: enmity transformed into friendship through good conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: Avot de-Rabbi Natan records the view that true might is the ability to make an enemy into a friend.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis and Valluvar both place the highest strength and greatness in converting enemies to friends.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23:1 (tr. A. Cohen, Soncino)

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha walked toward the feared bandit Angulimala, who was trying to kill him; through his words Angulimala laid down his weapons, became a monk, and later attained liberation.
buddhism.explanation: The most dangerous enemy of the region was transformed into a disciple and a friend of the Sangha.
buddhism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s ideal at its most dramatic: a deadly foe made into a friend.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of enemy-to-friend conversion; spiritual rather than political.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the end of Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena persuades the angry Furies, who threaten to blight Athens, to accept honour in the city; they become the Kindly Ones and bless the land instead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena turns implacable avengers into protectors through persuasion rather than force.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The city’s safety rests on this conversion, just as the Kural says the world rests on those who make foes into friends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit including the communal benefit; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius records the sage Cleobulus as advising that one should do good to friends to keep them friends, and to enemies to make them friends.
philosophy.explanation: One of the Seven Sages makes winning over enemies a deliberate aim of kindness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this practice of turning enemies into friends.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 1.91 (Cleobulus)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match; paraphrased and the attribution to Cleobulus is traditional.

kurals.tamil:
தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால் தான்ஒருவன்
இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thandhunai indraal pakaiyirantaal thaanoruvan
indhunaiyaak kolkavatrin ondru.
kurals.meaning: If you have no ally, face two enemies, and stand alone, make one of those two enemies into a friendly ally.
kurals.elementary: Suppose two bigger kids are both upset with you and nobody is on your side. Instead of fighting both, you make peace with one of them, and suddenly it is two against one in your favour. That is the smart move the poet recommends.
kurals.university: This is the most explicitly strategic couplet of the chapter. Three conditions are stacked in clipped clauses: taṉtuṇai iṉṟāl (‘if one has no support’), pakai iraṇṭāl (‘if the enemies are two’), tāṉ oruvaṉ (‘and one is alone’). The remedy is to take one of the two as iṉtuṇai (இன்துணை), a ‘sweet’ or agreeable ally. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a general maxim, while Solomon Pappaiah again frames it for a ruler; Sivayogi Sivakumar keeps it close to the text. It complements 874: where that couplet praised turning enemies into friends as a virtue, this one treats it as a necessity of statecraft, in line with the Indian political tradition of alliances among neighbouring powers. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra treats foreign policy as a circle of kings and recommends that a weaker king make peace or alliance (sandhi) with one power when he cannot stand against several.
hinduism.explanation: The classical Indian manual of statecraft makes alliance with one party a standard response to weakness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the same advice in miniature: alone against two, ally with one.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Doctrinal parallel in the same political tradition; summarized rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: A king who sees he is outmatched sends envoys to make peace before battle.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise advises turning a foe into a friend when one cannot win alone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Makes peace with one stronger foe; does not mention a second enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allāh. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the Prophet to accept peace when an adversary offers it.
islam.tie_back: Both texts endorse turning an adversary into a partner in peace when possible.
islam._accuracy_note: Supports making peace with an enemy; lacks the two-enemies strategic setting.

judaism.quote_or_event: Hunted by King Saul and without support in Israel, David went over to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, and lived under his protection.
judaism.explanation: Facing a deadly pursuer, David found safety by allying himself with another of Israel’s enemies.
judaism.tie_back: He acts out the Kural’s advice: alone and threatened, take one hostile power as an ally.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close narrative fit; the Philistines were Israel’s enemies rather than David’s personal foes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the account of the Buddha’s last days, King Ajatasattu’s minister Vassakara is sent to ask about attacking the Vajjians; the Buddha explains they cannot be defeated while united, and the tradition later relates that they were overcome after being divided.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows how dividing a set of opponents changes the balance of power.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the reverse side of the Kural’s strategy: separating two hostile parties so one can be won over.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Indirect; the sutta teaches communal unity, and the division of the Vajjians comes from later tradition.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the war against the Titans, Zeus freed the Hundred-Handers whom their father had imprisoned, and with them as allies he defeated the Titans.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus won a war he could not win alone by bringing estranged powers to his side.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s strategy of gaining an ally to tip the balance.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose fit: the Hundred-Handers were not Zeus’s own enemies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a prince gains respect by declaring himself openly for one side, and warns that neutrality usually leaves one prey to the winner.
philosophy.explanation: He advises taking an ally rather than standing alone between rival powers.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he sees lone neutrality between two threats as dangerous and alliance as the remedy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Related strategic logic; Machiavelli discusses siding in others’ wars, not befriending an enemy.

kurals.tamil:
தேறினும் தேறா விடினும் அழிவின்கண்
தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Therinum theraa vitinum azhivinkan
theraan pakaaan vital.
kurals.meaning: Whether or not you have tested and trusted a person before, in a time of crisis neither commit yourself to them nor break with them; keep a careful middle distance.
kurals.elementary: When something big goes wrong, it is not the time to suddenly make a new best friend or to start a new fight. The poet says: stay polite and keep a bit of distance, and wait until things are calm before deciding who to trust.
kurals.university: This is among the most compressed and debated couplets of the chapter. The verb tēṟu (தேறு, ‘to trust, be convinced about’) appears three times: tēṟiṉum tēṟā viṭiṉum (‘whether one has trusted him or not’), then tēṟāṉ (‘not trusting’) paired with pakāaṉ (பகாஅன், ‘not separating’, with the alapedai lengthening), ending in viṭal (‘leave him so’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: whether you had earlier assessed a man or not, in a time of ruin neither trust him nor drop him; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar apply it specifically to an enemy, advising neither closeness nor open rupture; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as ‘do not approach the untrustworthy in ruinous times’. Pope’s verse is loose, and his explanation ‘neither to join nor separate’ follows the traditional reading. The thirukkural.net English summary, ‘be wary of joining or opposing any’, captures the consensus: in crisis, keep a guarded neutrality. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the Kurukshetra war, Balarama, bound by affection to both the Pandavas and Duryodhana, refused to fight for either side and left on pilgrimage along the Sarasvati.
hinduism.explanation: In the greatest crisis of his family, Balarama neither joined nor broke with either party.
hinduism.tie_back: It is a living example of the Kural’s guarded middle course in a time of ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Shalya Parva
hinduism._accuracy_note: Illustrates neutrality in crisis; Balarama’s motive was affection for both, not caution about trust.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus counsels his disciples to combine wariness with harmlessness in a hostile world.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s advice is the same blend: neither trust blindly nor provoke a break.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the posture of guarded harmlessness; not specifically about crisis-time alliances.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, take your precaution and [either] go forth in companies or go forth all together.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an instructs believers facing danger to stay alert and take precautions.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly counsels caution rather than hasty trust in dangerous times.
islam._accuracy_note: General call to caution in conflict; does not address whom to trust or not break with.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah warns to be careful with the ruling powers, since they draw people close only for their own needs, seem like friends when it suits them, and do not stand by a person in the hour of distress.
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel’s teaching warns that apparent friends may vanish exactly when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: This is why the Kural advises not committing to anyone untested in a time of ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on unreliable allies in crisis; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha describes false friends, including the one who is a companion only in pleasure and the one who helps only out of self-interest, and contrasts them with the friend who stands by you in misfortune.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives criteria for telling true friends from false ones.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same problem: in crisis one cannot yet know who is true, so one should stay guarded.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Related teaching on testing friends; does not prescribe neutrality.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Trojans found the great wooden horse left by the Greeks, the priest Laocoön urged them not to trust it, saying he feared the Greeks even when they brought gifts.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the decisive moment, an untested offer from a former enemy was the most dangerous thing in Troy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns against committing to the untested in a time of danger, which is what Troy failed to heed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Roman telling of a Greek myth; illustrates distrust, not the middle course of neither joining nor breaking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the wish to be friends comes quickly but friendship does not; people cannot know each other until they have shared much over time.
philosophy.explanation: Trust has to be tested by time and experience, not assumed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies this to crisis: trust that has not been tested should not be relied on when ruin looms.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Supports caution about untested trust; Aristotle does not discuss crisis neutrality.

kurals.tamil:
நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு மேவற்க
மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Novarka nondhadhu ariyaarkku mevarka
menmai pakaivar akaththu.
kurals.meaning: Do not tell your troubles to those who do not already know of them, and do not show weakness in front of your enemies.
kurals.elementary: If you are feeling hurt, you do not have to tell everyone you meet. And if someone is being mean to you, try not to show them where it hurts, because they might poke you there again. Share your worries with the people who really care and already understand.
kurals.university: The couplet has two prohibitions in parallel: nōvaṟka (‘do not lament’) to those who do not know one’s suffering, and mēvaṟka (‘do not take on, display’) meṉmai (மென்மை, ‘softness, weakness’) in the presence of enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the first line as referring to friends who have not themselves perceived one’s distress: to complain to them is undignified and spreads knowledge of one’s weakness. Solomon Pappaiah reads the hidden object of both lines as ‘our lack of strength’, which should neither be told to unaware friends nor shown to enemies. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the lines quite differently: do not grieve over those who do not understand grief, and do not covet the soft spot of enemies. Pope’s ‘To those who know them not, complain not of your woes; nor to your foeman’s eyes infirmities disclose’ follows the majority reading. The text is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During their thirteenth year of exile, the Pandavas lived in disguise at King Virata’s court, enduring hardships and insults in silence so that the Kauravas could not discover them.
hinduism.explanation: Revealing themselves before the year ended would have handed their enemies the advantage.
hinduism.tie_back: They lived out the Kural’s rule: keep your suffering hidden and give your enemies no glimpse of weakness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good illustration of concealed hardship before enemies; driven by the exile terms, not only prudence.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus warns not to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before swine, lest they trample them and turn and tear you.
christianity.explanation: What is precious and vulnerable should not be exposed to those who will misuse it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the same caution to one’s sorrows and weaknesses.
christianity._accuracy_note: Adjacent principle of discretion; paraphrased and not about personal weakness.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: The prophet Jacob, grieving for Joseph, refuses to pour out his sorrow to those around him and takes it only to God; earlier in the same sura he warns Joseph not to tell his dream to his brothers lest they plot against him (12:5).
islam.tie_back: Together the verses mirror both halves of the Kural: do not air your grief to the unknowing, and do not expose yourself to hostile people.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on both halves, though Jacob’s restraint is devotional as well as prudent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That he told her all his heart, and said unto her. There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother’s womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.”
judaism.explanation: Samson revealed the secret of his weakness to Delilah, who was working for his Philistine enemies, and was captured.
judaism.tie_back: This is the classic disaster the Kural warns against: disclosing one’s weakness where enemies can use it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Precise narrative illustration of the second line.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kacchapa Jataka, a talkative tortoise carried through the air on a stick by two geese cannot resist answering the mocking children below, opens his mouth, and falls.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta uses the tale to teach a king the danger of speaking at the wrong moment.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that speaking out in front of those who mock you can be one’s undoing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: About untimely speech generally rather than revealing sorrow or weakness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus wakes on Ithaca, Athena disguises him as an old beggar and advises him to tell no one who he is and to endure in silence the insults of the suitors until the time is right.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus keeps his identity and his grief hidden from both enemies and most of his household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He follows the Kural to the letter, concealing pain and vulnerability from his foes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on concealment before enemies; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that in company one should avoid frequently and at length talking about one’s own actions and dangers, since others do not enjoy hearing them as much as one enjoys telling them.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic counsels reserve about one’s own troubles in ordinary society.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s first line about not airing sorrows to those who do not already know.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the first half (reserve about one’s troubles); nothing on hiding weakness from enemies.

kurals.tamil:
வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப மாயும்
பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu tharseydhu tharkaappa maayum
pakaivarkan patta serukku.
kurals.meaning: Know the right way to act, build up your own strength, and guard yourself well; then the arrogance of your enemies will fade away by itself.
kurals.elementary: If a team keeps teasing yours, the best answer is not to shout back but to practise, get stronger, and play smart. When they see how ready you are, their boasting stops on its own.
kurals.university: Three participial steps lead to the result: vakai aṟintu (‘knowing the method’), taṟceytu (‘making oneself strong’), taṟkāppa (‘guarding oneself’); then māyum (‘will perish’) the cerukku (செருக்கு, ‘pride, arrogance, exultation’) that has arisen in the enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read cerukku as the enemy’s pride, which collapses without a blow once one is prepared; Solomon Pappaiah adds that taṟkāppa includes guarding one’s secrets, linking back to 877; Pope’s explanation renders cerukku as the foes’ ‘joy’ and taṟceytu as ‘securing assistance’, a reading that ties the couplet to 875. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as knowing one’s qualifications and self-protection. The point is deterrence: preparation defeats an enemy’s confidence before any conflict. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s Arthashastra teaches that a king should first strengthen the constituent elements of his own state, such as treasury, army, fort and allies, since a well-fortified kingdom deters attack.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft makes self-strengthening the foundation of security against enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s sequence of knowing the method, strengthening oneself, and self-protection follows the same logic.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Doctrinal parallel summarized; not a direct quotation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to be fully equipped so that they can stand firm against their adversary.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that preparation and self-protection are what defeat an enemy’s schemes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Spiritual rather than political armour, but the logic of preparedness matches.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allāh and your enemy...”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to build up their strength so that enemies are deterred.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: preparation itself breaks the enemy’s confidence.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on strength as deterrence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.”
judaism.explanation: Mocked and threatened by Sanballat and his allies, Nehemiah’s builders worked and stood guard at once until the wall was finished, and their enemies lost heart.
judaism.tie_back: They did what the Kural advises: knew what to do, made themselves strong, and guarded themselves, and the enemies’ arrogance collapsed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel, including the enemies’ deflation at the end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada urges one to see the body as fragile as a clay pot, to make the mind secure like a fortified city, and to fight Mara with the weapon of wisdom.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a well-defended city for inner preparedness against the adversary.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s self-fortification against outer foes has an inner counterpart here.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before facing Medusa, Perseus learned the way from the Graeae and the nymphs and equipped himself with winged sandals, a cap of invisibility, a pouch and a sickle, so that he could approach and escape safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Perseus succeeded because he first learned the method and armed himself well.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This follows the Kural’s order: know the way, make yourself ready, protect yourself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates preparation; the Gorgon’s ‘pride’ is not the issue in the myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu teaches that skilled warriors of old first made themselves invincible and then waited for the enemy to become vulnerable; securing against defeat lies in one’s own hands.
philosophy.explanation: Strategy begins with one’s own preparation, not with attacking.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise places victory over an enemy’s arrogance in one’s own readiness.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 4 (tr. Lionel Giles)

kurals.tamil:
இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க களையுநர்
கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilaidhaaka mulmaram kolka kalaiyunar
kaikollum kaazhththa itaththu.
kurals.meaning: Cut down a thorny tree while it is still young; once it has hardened, it will wound the hand of the one who tries to remove it.
kurals.elementary: A tiny thorny weed in the garden can be pulled out with two fingers. If you leave it for a year, it grows big, tough thorns that scratch your hands when you finally try to pull it. Problems are the same: deal with them while they are small.
kurals.university: The couplet is a pure agricultural image applied to enmity, as all the commentators make explicit: iḷaitāka (‘while young’) muḷmaram (முள்மரம், ‘thorn tree’) kolka (‘destroy’); otherwise, kāḻtta iṭattu (‘when it has hardened’, from kāḻ, the hard heartwood) it kai kollum (‘destroys the hand’) of the kaḷaiyunar (களையுநர், ‘those who weed it out’). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the literal image; Kalaignar draws the lesson that enmity must be put down before it matures; Sivayogi Sivakumar adds the explicit note that enmity must not be allowed to grow. Solomon Pappaiah reads the thorn tree as one who intends to destroy us. The verb kol- (‘kill’) appears in both lines, giving a pointed reversal: kill it, or it kills your hand. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Duryodhana’s birth, ill omens appeared, and Vidura and the Brahmins advised Dhritarashtra to abandon the child for the sake of the family; out of affection he refused, and the conflict that followed destroyed the Kuru line.
hinduism.explanation: The epic presents a danger recognised early and left to grow until it consumed everyone.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s thorn tree left uncut, wounding the very hands that later tried to remove it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the advice concerned an infant, so the parallel should be read only at the level of foreseen danger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces how a small inner impulse grows step by step into something deadly.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts warn that what is small and manageable now becomes lethal once full grown.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same growth-to-danger logic, applied to sin rather than enmity.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against the first small steps of wrongdoing, which lead on to greater harm.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges stopping a danger at its first stage.
islam._accuracy_note: Indirect: about gradual temptation rather than enmity growing.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the evil inclination is at first like a spider’s thread, but in the end it becomes like the thick ropes of a wagon.
judaism.explanation: What begins as something easily broken becomes, if left alone, something that cannot be broken.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same image of early weakness and later strength as the Kural’s young and hardened thorn tree.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close image of growth from weak to unbreakable; paraphrased, and applied to inner evil rather than enemies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a tree, though cut down, sprouts up again if its roots remain uncut and firm, even so, until the craving that lies dormant is rooted out, suffering springs up again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a tree image to teach that a danger must be removed at the root or it returns.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also uses a tree to teach thorough, timely removal of what will harm you.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared tree metaphor; emphasis is on roots rather than timing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Paris was born, Hecuba dreamed she gave birth to a firebrand that set Troy ablaze; the seer warned of the danger, but the child survived, grew up, and his abduction of Helen brought about the city’s destruction.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a foretold danger not dealt with in time, which grows into the ruin of all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s warning that what is left to mature will destroy those who later try to handle it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic parallel at the level of foreseen and neglected danger; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli compares political troubles to a wasting fever, which at first is easy to cure but hard to detect, and later easy to detect but hard to cure; the Romans, he says, dealt with troubles as soon as they foresaw them.
philosophy.explanation: A wise ruler acts on dangers early, while they are still small.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thorn tree turned into a theory of statecraft.

kurals.tamil:
உயிர்ப்ப உளரல்லர் மன்ற செயிர்ப்பவர்
செம்மல் சிதைக்கலா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uyirppa ularallar mandra seyirppavar
semmal sidhaikkalaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who fail to break the pride of hostile enemies certainly cannot be said to live, not even to the extent of drawing breath.
kurals.elementary: If someone keeps bullying a group and nobody ever stands up to them, the bully only gets bolder. The poet says that people who never stand up to proud, hostile enemies are not really living freely at all.
kurals.university: The closing couplet is the chapter’s sharpest. Uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘so much as to breathe’) uḷar allar (‘they do not exist’) maṉṟa (மன்ற, ‘certainly’): such people are not alive even to breathe. The condition is that they cannot citaikkal (‘shatter’) the cemmal (செம்மல், ‘pride, eminence, haughtiness’) of ceyirppavar (செயிர்ப்பவர், ‘those who are hostile or offend’). Kalaignar reads it as: those who cannot break the enemies’ arrogance cannot truly be called alive just because they breathe; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that such people will be destroyed within a breath; Mu. Varadarasanar’s printed gloss on ytamizh reads ‘தலைமையைக் கொடுக்க’, which appears to be a typographic slip for கெடுக்க (‘destroy’). Sivayogi Sivakumar takes ceyirppavar as open wrongdoers. Read with 871 and 874, the chapter’s logic is clear: never seek enmity, convert it where possible, but where it persists, deal with it decisively. The text matches in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rouses Arjuna from paralysis on the battlefield and tells him to face his opponents.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats failure to confront hostile pride as a kind of living death.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong call to confront enemies; the Gita frames it as duty, not survival.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the Magnificat, Mary praises God who has shown strength with his arm and scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
christianity.explanation: The song celebrates the overthrow of the arrogant.
christianity.tie_back: It echoes the Kural’s concern with breaking the pride of the hostile, though as God’s act rather than a human duty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak match: divine action against the proud, not human resolve; paraphrased.

islam.quote_or_event: “Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allāh is competent to give them victory.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an permits the wronged to defend themselves against those who attack them.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it accepts that aggressive enemies sometimes must be confronted.
islam._accuracy_note: Permission for self-defence rather than a statement that failing to resist is a living death.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the Philistine said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together.”
judaism.explanation: For forty days Goliath’s challenge paralysed Israel, until young David went out and brought down his pride.
judaism.tie_back: Israel’s paralysis before Goliath is the condition the Kural calls not truly living, and David’s act is its remedy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit with a defiant enemy whose pride is broken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who conquers himself is a greater victor than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand men in battle.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism relocates the real battle from outer enemies to one’s own mind.
buddhism.tie_back: It offers a contrasting view to the Kural’s call to break the enemy’s pride: the pride to break first is one’s own.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel; Buddhism does not advise crushing enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning home after twenty years, Odysseus strings his bow and, with Telemachus, overcomes the arrogant suitors who had been consuming his household and plotting against his son.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic’s climax is the breaking of the suitors’ insolence by the rightful master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It enacts the Kural’s demand that the pride of hostile enemies must be broken.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on overcoming arrogant foes; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that men should either be treated well or be crushed, because they can avenge slight injuries but not serious ones.
philosophy.explanation: He warns that half-measures against enemies leave them able to strike back.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that those who leave hostile pride intact will not survive.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in strategic logic, though harsher in tone; paraphrased.
